questions.question: In the diagram shown below, L1 is an Ethernet LAN and L2 is a Token-Ring LAN. An IP packet originates from sender S and traverses to R, as shown. The links within each ISP and across the two ISPs, are all point-to-point' optical links. The initial value of the TTL field is 32. The maximum possible value of the TTL field when R receives the datagram is ____________.
questions.explanation:
TTL is decremented only by routers (layer 3). The bridges/switches inside LAN L1 and the stations on token ring L2 work at layer 2 and do not touch TTL.

Following the path, the datagram passes through 6 routers (the square boxes).

TTL at R = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 6 = 26

Answer: 26

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct about HTTP cookies?

options.A: A cookie is a piece of code that has the potential to compromise the security of an Internet user
options.B: A cookie gains entry to the user's work area through an HTTP header
options.C: A cookie has an expiry date and time
options.D: Cookies can be used to track the browsing pattern of a user at a particular site

questions.explanation:
A cookie is a small piece of data (name-value text) stored by the browser, not executable code.

It does come in the Set-Cookie HTTP header, has an expiry time and can track browsing on a site.

Answer: A cookie is a piece of code that has the potential to compromise security

questions.question: Suppose that everyone in a group of N people wants to communicate secretly with the N-1 others using symmetric key cryptographic system. The communication between any two persons should not be decodable by the others in the group. The number of keys required in the system as a whole to satisfy the confidentiality requirement is
questions.explanation:
Each pair of people needs its own shared secret key.

Number of pairs = [latex]\binom N2=\frac{N(N-1)}{2}[/latex]

Answer: N(N-1)/2

questions.question: Assume that source S and destination D are connected through two intermediate routers labeled R. Determine how many times each packet has to visit the network layer and the data link layer during a transmission from S to D.

options.A: Network layer - 4 times and Data link layer - 4 times
options.B: Network layer - 4 times and Data link layer - 3 times
options.C: Network layer - 4 times and Data link layer - 6 times
options.D: Network layer - 2 times and Data link layer - 6 times

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Network layer: at S, both routers, and D = 4 times
- Data link layer: S (send) + 2 per router (receive and send) + D (receive) = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6 times

Answer: Network layer 4 times and Data link layer 6 times

questions.question:
Node X has a TCP connection open to node Y. The packets from X to Y go through an intermediate IP router R. Ethernet switch S is the first switch on the network path between X and R. Consider a packet sent from X to Y over this connection.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the destination IP and MAC addresses on this packet at the time it leaves X?

options.A: The destination IP address is the IP address of R
options.B: The destination IP address is the IP address of Y
options.C: The destination MAC address is the MAC address of S
options.D: The destination MAC address is the MAC address of Y

questions.explanation:
Recall how addresses change along the path:
- IP addresses are end-to-end: the destination IP stays the IP of Y on the whole path.
- MAC addresses are hop-by-hop: the destination MAC is that of the next IP hop, which is router R. A switch only forwards frames; it is never the destination MAC.

So the only true statement is: destination IP = IP of Y.

Answer: The destination IP address is the IP address of Y

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation is/are TRUE?

options.A: The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed only at the source of the datagram
options.B: The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed at any IP router which finds that the size of the datagram to be transmitted exceeds the MTU
options.C: The reassembly of fragments is performed only at the destination of the datagram
options.D: The reassembly of fragments is performed at all intermediate routers along the path from the source to the destination

questions.explanation:
Recall the IPv4 fragmentation rules:
- In IPv4, any router whose outgoing link MTU is smaller than the datagram can fragment it (not only the source).
- Fragments may take different routes, so reassembly is done only at the destination.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.question:
Which one of the following is TRUE about the interior gateway routing protocols - Routing
Information Protocol (RIP) and Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)?

options.A: RIP uses distance vector routing and OSPF uses link state routing
options.B: OSPF uses distance vector routing and RIP uses link state routing
options.C: Both RIP and OSPF use link state routing
options.D: Both RIP and OSPF use distance vector routing

questions.explanation:
RIP shares distance vectors with neighbours (Bellman-Ford). OSPF floods link-state advertisements and runs Dijkstra.

Answer: RIP uses distance vector routing and OSPF uses link state routing

questions.question:
Consider a file of size [latex]4[/latex] million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth [latex]2[/latex] Mbps , [latex]500[/latex] kbps , and [latex]1[/latex] Mbps , respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file.

Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file?
Note: [latex]1 {M}=10^{6}, 1 {k}=10^{3}[/latex]
questions.explanation:
With processing and propagation delays negligible, the effective throughput of a series of links is limited by the slowest (bottleneck) link in the path — here, [latex]500[/latex] kbps (since it's the minimum of [latex]2[/latex] Mbps, [latex]500[/latex] kbps, and [latex]1[/latex] Mbps).

File size [latex]=4\times10^6[/latex] bytes [latex]=4\times10^6\times8=32\times10^6[/latex] bits.

Total transfer time [latex]=\dfrac{32\times10^6\text{ bits}}{500\times10^3\text{ bps}}=64[/latex] seconds.

Answer: 64

questions.question:
An IP datagram of size 1000 bytes arrives at a router. The router has to forward this packet on a link whose MTU (maximum transmission unit)is 100bytes. Assume that the size of the IP header is 20bytes.
The number of fragments that the IP datagram will be divided into for transmission is _________.
questions.explanation:
Data = 1000 [latex]-[/latex] 20 = 980 bytes. Per fragment: 100 [latex]-[/latex] 20 = 80 bytes of data (already a multiple of 8).

Fragments = [latex]\lceil980/80\rceil=\lceil12.25\rceil=13[/latex]

Answer: 13

questions.question:
Consider an Ethernet segment with a transmission speed of [latex]10^8[/latex] bits/sec and a
maximum segment length of 500 meters. If the speed of propagation of the signal
in the medium is [latex]2 \times 10^8[/latex] meters/sec, then the minimum frame size (in bits) required
for collision detection is _________
questions.explanation:
For collision detection, transmission time must be at least the round-trip propagation time: [latex]\frac{L}{B}\ge2\frac{d}{v}[/latex]

[latex]T_p=\dfrac{500}{2\times10^8}=2.5\ \mu s[/latex]

[latex]L=2\times2.5\times10^{-6}\times10^8=500[/latex] bits

Answer: 500

questions.question: An IP router with a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of 1500 bytes has received an IP packet of size 4404 bytes with an IP header of length 20 bytes. The values of the relevant fields in the header of the third IP fragment generated by the router for this packet are

- Fragment 1: 1480 B, offset 0
- Fragment 2: 1480 B, offset 185
- Fragment 3: 4384 [latex]-[/latex] 2960 = 1424 B, offset 2960 / 8 = 370, last fragment so MF = 0

Datagram length = 1424 + 20 = 1444

Answer: MF bit: 0, Datagram Length: 1444, Offset: 370

questions.question:
Consider an instance of TCP's Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD) algorithm where
the window size at the start of the slow start phase is 2 MSS and the threshold at the start of the first
transmission is 8 MSS. Assume that a timeout occurs during the fifth transmission. Find the
congestion window size at the end of the tenth transmission.
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Transmissions 1-3 (slow start): 2, 4, 8 (threshold reached)
- 4, 5: 9, 10 (additive increase), timeout during the 5th
- New threshold = 10/2 = 5, window restarts at 2
- 6: 2, 7: 4, 8: 5 (capped at the threshold), 9: 6, 10: 7

Answer: 7 MSS

questions.question:
Consider a network path [latex]\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R} [/latex] between nodes [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{R} [/latex] via router [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Node [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] sends a file of size [latex]10^6 [/latex] bytes to [latex]R [/latex] via this path by splitting the file into chunks of [latex]10^3 [/latex] bytes each. Node [latex]P [/latex] sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.
Each of the links [latex]\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q} [/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R} [/latex] has a bandwidth of [latex]10^6 \mathrm{bits} / \mathrm{sec} [/latex], and negligible propagation latency. Router [latex]Q [/latex] immediately transmits every packet it receives from [latex]P [/latex] to [latex]R [/latex], with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router [latex]Q [/latex] can simultaneously receive on link [latex]P-Q [/latex] and transmit on [latex]\operatorname{link} Q-R [/latex].
Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time [latex]t=0 [/latex]. Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which [latex]\mathrm{R} [/latex] receives all the chunks of the file?
questions.explanation:
Number of chunks [latex]=10^6/10^3=1000[/latex]. Each chunk [latex]=8000[/latex] bits, so transmission time on a link [latex]=\frac{8000}{10^6}=8[/latex] ms.

P sends the chunks back to back: the last chunk is fully sent by P at [latex]1000\times8\text{ ms}=8[/latex] s.
Q forwards each chunk while receiving the next, so only the last chunk adds one more transmission of 8 ms on Q-R.

Total [latex]=8+0.008=8.008[/latex] s.

Answer: 8.008

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question: For a host machine that uses the token bucket algorithm for congestion control, the token bucket has a capacity of 1 megabyte and the maximum output rate is 20 megabytes per second. Tokens arrive at a rate to sustain output at a rate of 10megabytes per second. The  token bucket is currently full and the machine needs to send 12megabytes of data. The minimum time required to transmit the data is _____seconds.
questions.explanation:
Bucket starts full (1 MB). While it drains, the host sends at 20 MB/s while tokens arrive at 10 MB/s:
[latex]20t=1+10t\Rightarrow t=0.1[/latex] s, sending 2 MB.

The remaining 10 MB go at 10 MB/s = 1 s.

Total = 0.1 + 1 = 1.1 s

Answer: 1.1

questions.question:
Consider an IP packet with a length of 4,500 bytes that includes a 20-byte IPv4 header and a 40-byte TCP header. The packet is forwarded to an IPv4 router that supports a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of 600 bytes. Assume that the length of the IP header in all the outgoing fragments of this packet is 20 bytes. Assume that the fragmentation offset value stored in the first fragment is 0.
The fragmentation offset value stored in the third fragment is _______.
questions.explanation:
Data = 4500 [latex]-[/latex] 20 = 4480 bytes. Each fragment carries 600 [latex]-[/latex] 20 = 580, rounded down to a multiple of 8: 576 bytes.

Offsets (in 8-byte units): fragment 1 = 0, fragment 2 = 576/8 = 72, fragment 3 = 1152/8 = 144.

Answer: 144

questions.question: Consider a network using the pure ALOHA medium access control protocol, where each frame is of length 1,000 bits. The channel transmission rate is 1 Mbps (=[latex]10^6[/latex] bits per second). The aggregate number of transmissions across all the nodes (including new frame transmissions and retransmitted frames due to collisions) is modelled as a Poisson process with a rate of 1,000 frames per second. Throughput is defined as the average number of frames successfully transmitted per second. The throughput of the network (rounded to the nearest integer) is ______________
questions.explanation:
Frame time T = 1000 / [latex]10^6[/latex] = 1 ms. Load G = 1000 frames/s [latex]\times[/latex] 1 ms = 1.

Pure ALOHA success probability = [latex]e^{-2G}=e^{-2}\approx0.135[/latex].
Throughput = 1000 [latex]\times[/latex] 0.135 [latex]\approx[/latex] 135 frames/s

Answer: 135

questions.question: Consider a 100 Mbps link between an earth station (sender) and a satellite (receiver) at an altitude of 2100 km. The signal propagates at a speed of [latex]3  \times 10^8[/latex] m/s. The time taken (in milliseconds, rounded off to two decimal places) for the receiver to completely receive a packet of 1000 bytes transmitted by the sender is
questions.explanation:
Total time = transmission time + propagation time.
- Transmission time [latex]=\frac{1000\times8}{100\times10^6}=0.08[/latex] ms
- Propagation time [latex]=\frac{2100\times10^3}{3\times10^8}=7[/latex] ms

Total [latex]=0.08+7=7.08[/latex] ms

Answer: 7.08

questions.question:
A packet with the destination IP address 145.36.109.70 arrives at a router whose routing table is shown. Which interface will the packet be forwarded to?
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Subnet Address} & \textbf{Subnet Mask (in CIDR notation)} & \textbf{Interface} \\ \hline 145.36.0.0 & /16 & E1 \\ \hline 145.36.128.0 & /17 & E2 \\ \hline 145.36.64.0 & /18 & E3 \\ \hline 145.36.255.0 & /24 & E4 \\ \hline \text{Default} & -- & E5 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
questions.explanation:
Routers use longest-prefix matching: find every subnet entry that contains the destination address, and among those, forward via the one with the most specific (longest) prefix.

Destination: [latex]145.36.109.70[/latex]. Check each entry:
- [latex]145.36.0.0/16[/latex] (E1): matches any [latex]145.36.x.x[/latex] — matches.
- [latex]145.36.128.0/17[/latex] (E2): covers 3rd octet [latex]128[/latex]-[latex]255[/latex]; our 3rd octet is [latex]109[/latex] — no match.
- [latex]145.36.64.0/18[/latex] (E3): covers 3rd octet [latex]64[/latex]-[latex]127[/latex]; [latex]109[/latex] falls in this range — matches.
- [latex]145.36.255.0/24[/latex] (E4): only [latex]145.36.255.x[/latex]; no match.

Between the two matches (E1's [latex]/16[/latex] and E3's [latex]/18[/latex]), the [latex]/18[/latex] is more specific (longer prefix), so it wins.

Answer: E3
